cover.family: Sierramont Middle School, San Jose, CA

profile.title: Neerav at a Glance
profile.lead: Neerav U., eighth grade at Sierramont Middle School, San Jose. What he does, and how he works.

blocks.thesis: He runs a Pokemon-card business with customers, and it has a goal attached.
blocks.body: He buys and sells Pokemon cards outside school, about four to six hours a week, and it makes a few thousand dollars a year. The goal his mother describes is to find cards that can be kept and become valuable enough to pay for a semester of college tuition, $5,000 to $10,000. Before this he ran an in-game Roblox business selling to other kids. Asked what he loves, he answers running my business and debating ideas.

blocks.thesis: He competes across several areas, and tends to place when he does.
blocks.body: He has won medals in chess tournaments. He was a top-five finalist with a medal at a district-level cooking competition. He has played ping-pong for one to two years, one to three hours a week, and would like to try tennis instead. He performed in two elementary-school musicals. His interests run wider: writing and journalism, music, debate, business, languages and culture, history and politics, philosophy. He travelled to India, including the Ladakh mountains, river rafting and zip-lining, and wrote about that trip, and to France and on an African safari.

blocks.thesis: He makes friends easily and people seek him out, which is where being able to lead a group starts.
blocks.body: He gets along with people and works well in a group. His mother names Leader among the words that describe him. He learns by listening and discussion. He thinks by debating: he takes apart something in politics or business, asks what if we did this versus that, and compares the outcomes. He works best when the concept is taught before it is tested, when instructions are clear, when there are milestones, and when a mistake has a route back, such as a retake.

blocks.subhead: What is in his favour, and what shapes the choices
blocks.thesis: A university-educated household, a first-generation American background, and money he already earns himself.
blocks.body: His mother holds a Columbia University degree and his stepfather is a scientist at Stanford — an academic household, though neither is a tie to any of the six schools on his list. He is a first-generation American from an immigrant family; because his mother holds a college degree, that is background rather than a first-in-family-to-college advantage. He lives in San Jose, inside the University of California's home state, and in his own words he is open to all cultures and foods. Two things shape the choices: a focused set of commitments he can sustain well, and in-person activity close to home, with autumn dates preferred because spring brings a long allergy season his mother describes as debilitating.

profile.flags: A few things to confirm with Neerav: the six colleges listed here, and roughly how many hours a week chess, cooking and theatre take. It would also help to know which organisation ran the chess tournaments and the district cooking competition, since that decides what those results can be entered into later.

cards.title: Check the weaker subject against class tests

cards.body: A slip found in March can still be turned around.

cards.plan_by: By early March, at the first term tests.

terms.tag: A light summer is the right answer
terms.intro: On the summer after eighth grade: a light one is entirely fine at this age. His own trading, the family service commitment and the ninth-grade placement, not a purchased programme.

cards.title: Settle the ninth-grade placement
cards.act: Take the strongest math and English placement he can carry well.
cards.body: Placement decides which sequences stay open for four years, and is hard to undo.
cards.contact: The high school counsellor, once registration opens.
cards.plan_by: Ask the counsellor in January for the registration date.
cards.note: Strongest he can carry well, not strongest available.

cards.title: A longer stretch with the same organisation
cards.act: Give the organisation more hours while school is not competing.
cards.body: The summer is where a family commitment gets its depth.
cards.contact: The volunteer coordinator at the organisation.
cards.plan_by: By May, because summer slots are agreed before term ends.
cards.note: He keeps trading at the hours he already gives it.

parent_actions.lead: Ordered by when you need to act, not by importance.

items.text: Register the booth for the Santa Clara Children's Business Fair, and confirm his age against the 6 to 14 band at the same time.
Ask the Sierramont office whether the school fields a speech and debate club, and which formats it runs.
Ask the school for the recent report card and identify the weakest or underperforming subjects.
Ask the San Jose business tax office and the Santa Clara County clerk-recorder what a business run by someone his age has to file.
Note which organisation ran the chess tournaments his medals came from, and roughly how many hours a week chess, cooking and theatre take.
Ask him whether he still cooks and competes, and whether he would want cooking entered through school later.
Visit one or two local organisations that take families volunteering together, and commit to one.
Confirm the six colleges and the graduating class year, and check the financial aid position at each college on the list.
Confirm whether his high school runs a DECA or FBLA chapter, and which debate league its team competes in.

final_note: You wrote that he has a real business and real potential, and that what you do not want is that energy scattered. This plan is built to the same view. It adds nothing he did not already choose: the business stays exactly as it is, debate is where his own words already point, and the volunteering is the thing you asked for. Everything else he does is protected and asked nothing of.

The first steps are deliberately small and finishable. A one-day fair in October has a clear beginning and end. Sampling debate formats commits him to nothing. Where a result is involved, it comes through a coached team with many rounds and practice in between, so one round never decides anything on its own. The number of activities he carries is capped at two or three, and that choice is made in tenth grade, with a year and a half of trying things first. He is good at this when he has picked it himself and someone is behind him; the plan is arranged so both stay true.

tiers_note: These are each school's own published admit rate for its most recent class — how selective the school is, not Neerav's chance of getting in. We do not print a personal percentage, because nothing we hold can honestly produce one for an eighth grader. The tiers are the same on both plans: a school's selectivity does not move because a student works harder. What the Stretch changes is what he has to show, not the odds he faces. The finding here is the two empty columns — five of these six schools admit under one applicant in eight, and there is plenty of time to add schools where the answer is more likely to be yes.
